label: Leaving for College
framing: You are leaving the house you were formed in to become someone in a place no one knows you. Scripture honors the young who carry their faith into new and testing ground, and it tells them the one thing the campus will try to talk them out of, that the fear of the Lord, not the cleverness of the lecture hall, is where wisdom actually begins.
cultural: Our culture treats college as the time to leave faith behind with childhood, a rite of passage into a supposedly freer life. The Bible knows the opposite, that the years of youth are the time to remember your Creator, not forget him, and that a faith never owned for oneself, only inherited, will not survive the first real challenge to it.
historical: Daniel, taken as a youth into the schools of Babylon around 600 BC, learned the empire's books without bowing to the empire's gods, the model of a young believer who engaged the culture without being swallowed by it. The very universities of the West were founded by the church as places to seek truth under God, and across the centuries countless young Christians have found, in the testing of college, that their faith grew sturdier for being questioned.
application: Find a church and a community of believers within the first weeks, before isolation and the crowd do their work, since no one keeps the faith alone on a campus built to erode it. Decide your convictions now, in advance, rather than in the moment of pressure. Ask hard questions out loud and chase the answers, for honest faith is not afraid of the lecture hall. And keep the habits, prayer, Scripture, and worship, that hold a soul in a new place.

verses.text: But Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine. So he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself.
verses.where: Daniel and his friends are taken to Babylon as young men, given new names and trained in the language and literature of the Chaldeans for the king's service. They learn it all, and verse 17 says God gave them understanding in every kind of literature. The one place Daniel draws a line is the king's table. Faithfulness here is not refusing to learn; it is knowing where you will not bend.

verses.text: Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come and the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,” before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain, on the day the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop, when those grinding cease because they are few and those watching through windows see dimly, when the doors to the street are shut and the sound of the mill fades away, when one rises at the sound of a bird and all the daughters of song grow faint, when men fear the heights and dangers of the road, when the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper loses its spring, and the caper berry shrivels— for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets.
verses.where: The Teacher tells the young to remember their Creator before the hard years come, and then describes old age as a house falling silent. To remember, in Scripture, is more than recalling a fact. It is to live in the light of the one remembered, starting now.

verses.text: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
verses.where: Between Wisdom's banquet and Folly's loud invitation, Proverbs repeats its foundation: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. The fear meant here is reverent awe, the posture of a creature before its Maker. It does not compete with learning. It is where learning begins.

verses.text: Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.” When Jacob woke up, he thought, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.”
verses.where: Jacob leaves home alone, sleeps in the open with a stone for a pillow, and dreams of a stairway between earth and heaven. The note says God's promise turns personal: I am with you and will watch over you wherever you go. Jacob wakes saying the LORD was in this place and he did not know it.

verses.text: If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle by the farthest sea, even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast.
verses.where: David asks where he could go to escape God's presence and answers that there is nowhere: not the heavens, not the far edge of the sea. Even there God's hand will guide him. A new city where no one knows your name is not a place God has never been.

verses.text: He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed.
verses.where: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, and the companion of fools comes to harm. The friends made in the first months away from home often shape the years that follow. Proverbs says to choose them on purpose.

verses.text: And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.
verses.where: Hebrews tells believers to hold fast their hope, to think about how to stir one another to love and good works, and not to give up meeting together as some had. It is not written to students, but it names the habit that often disappears first when a young person leaves home: belonging to a church.

verses.text: Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true.
verses.where: At Berea, Paul's hearers received his message eagerly and examined the Scriptures every day to see if what he said was true. Luke calls them noble-minded for it. Testing what you are taught, including what you are taught about the faith, is not disloyalty; Scripture praises it.

verses.text: But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ.
verses.where: Peter writes to believers living among neighbors who did not share their faith. He tells them to be ready to give a reason for their hope to anyone who asks, and to do it with gentleness and respect. The answer and the manner both matter, and a clear conscience speaks loudest.

verses.text: For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.
verses.where: In Athens, a city of philosophers, Paul begins from an altar and a poet the Athenians already knew. The site's plain note says many read him as taking his hearers' questions and best thinkers seriously, while still calling them to repent and naming the resurrection they would find absurd. He met a learned city with courtesy and with conviction at once.

links.label: Practical guides for the inner life

misread.taken: Do not be conformed to this world is sometimes used to teach students that the university is the world, so that every hard class, unfamiliar idea or friend outside the church is a threat to be kept at arm's length.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says Paul does not tell believers to withdraw from society or call everything outside the church bad: the same letter tells them to live at peace with everyone and do what is right in everyone's eyes, and Paul worked at a trade and lived in cities. This world means the pattern of life that ignores God, not the created world or its people. What the verse asks is a mind being renewed, able to test and approve God's will, not a list of things to avoid.
misread.text: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

whole: Leaving for college is one of the largest changes many people ever make, and it happens at eighteen, often all at once. A new room, a new city, a schedule no one checks, and a freedom that is exciting and lonely in the same week. For a student raised in the church there is often a second change underneath: for the first time faith is not supported by family habit, and it meets professors and friends who see the world very differently. Some find their faith grows; some find it quietly drifts; some find hard questions they were never allowed to ask.

Scripture has been here before. Daniel and his friends were young when they were taken to the most learned city of their world and trained in its literature for the king's service. They learned it all, and stayed faithful. Jacob left home alone and met God on the road. The Bereans tested what they heard against the Scriptures and were praised for it. What usually carries a young person away from faith is less often a single argument than the slow loss of the things that held it: worship with others, honest friends, prayer that is one's own. Most of us drift more than we decide.

So the wisdom here is to go deliberately. Learn eagerly; nothing true is a threat to the God who made everything, and the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, not a reason to stop thinking. Know in advance where your Babylon table is, the few things you will not do, and decide them before the first weekend. Find a church in the first month, before the habit of Sunday sleep forms, and find a few friends who are walking with God. When hard questions come, take them seriously and bring them into the light, to Scripture, to wiser Christians, and to the long memory of the church, which has met most of them before. And be ready to give a reason for your hope with gentleness, to people who will become your friends.

Underneath it is the promise God gave a young man sleeping on a stone: I am with you and will watch over you wherever you go. Your faith does not have to be finished to be real; Daniel was still young, and so was Timothy. If you drift, the way back is open. If you stay, you may find that the questions you feared were the ones that made your faith your own.
deep.sit: What is the one thing you will decide now, before you arrive, so that you do not have to decide it the first weekend?

prayer.lead: Two verses of David asking to be shown God's paths and taught his truth, for anyone starting somewhere new.
prayer.text: Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths. Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; all day long I wait for You.
